client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it the way I used to — I keep noticing the empty chair where she used to sit, and it makes the whole thing feel hollow. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd try something.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you doubts it will help, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — that quiet, hollow ache at gatherings — makes complete sense after losing someone so central to your family. Grief has a way of reshaping familiar places, and noticing her absence in that empty chair sounds like a painful reminder that things have changed. I'm wondering, when you're sitting there and that feeling washes over you, what kinds of thoughts tend to run through your mind in that moment?

client: It's mostly thoughts like... "she should be here" or "nothing is ever going to feel normal again." And then I start wondering if everyone else is just moving on fine and I'm the only one still stuck, which makes me feel even more isolated, like there's something wrong with me for not being able to just enjoy being with family anymore. It's like I'm grieving in a room full of people who've already closed that door.
therapist: That image of grieving alone in a room full of people is such a poignant way to describe it, and I can hear how isolating that feels — like you're somehow out of step with everyone around you. I'd gently want to invite you to examine that thought that others have "already moved on," because grief is often much more private than it appears on the surface, and the people around you may be carrying their own quiet pain behind their smiles. What do you think might shift for you if it turned out others were also still struggling, just not showing it?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that, but honestly it feels a little like wishful thinking. Like, even if other people are struggling privately, that doesn't really change the fact that I'm still sitting here alone with it, you know? It's hard to feel connected to someone else's hidden pain when all I can see is their surface.
therapist: You're pushing back on that in a really honest way, and you're right — knowing others might be hurting doesn't automatically dissolve your own sense of loneliness in that moment. What you're describing points to something worth exploring: there's a difference between the thought "I'm alone with this" and the actual possibility of connection, and sometimes grief can act like a filter that makes distance feel more certain than it really is. I'm curious — has there been anyone in your family, even once, where you've caught a glimpse of something beneath their surface that suggested they might be feeling it too?

client: Yeah, actually... there was this one moment with my brother at the funeral. He didn't say much, but at one point he just kind of stared at my dad's photo for a long time, and when he finally looked away his eyes were red. I remember thinking he looked almost lost, but then he kind of shut down again and we never talked about it, and I guess I just filed it away as something that didn't really mean anything.
therapist: That moment with your brother sounds like it meant more than you've been giving it credit for — two people standing in the same grief, close enough to touch it, and yet the door stayed closed between you. It's interesting that your mind filed it away as "not meaning anything," when what you just described is actually a really tender glimpse of his pain. What do you think held you back from reaching toward each other in that moment, and do you think that door might still be open?

client: I guess I never thought of it that way — like we were both just standing there holding the same thing but too scared to say it out loud. What held me back was probably this fear that if I said something, it would either come out wrong or he'd shut me down, and then it would feel even worse than saying nothing at all. As for whether the door's still open... I honestly don't know, we haven't really talked since the funeral and I keep telling myself he probably needs space, but maybe that's just an excuse I'm using so I don't have to risk being rejected by him.
therapist: That last part you said — recognizing that "he needs space" might actually be a way of protecting yourself from the risk of rejection — that's a really significant and honest insight, and it takes courage to see that in yourself. What you're describing is a very human pattern: we sometimes frame avoidance as consideration for others, when underneath it's really about keeping ourselves safe from a pain that already feels like too much. I'm wondering, if you could imagine a version of that conversation with your brother going well, what would you most want him to know?

client: I guess... if it went well, I'd want him to know that I miss him. That it's not that I stopped caring — it's more like I got so tangled up in the guilt about how things fell apart that I just froze. But even imagining that conversation going well feels almost dangerous, like I'm setting myself up, because what if I say all that and he just... doesn't feel the same way?
therapist: There's something really moving about what you just shared — that underneath the distance isn't indifference, but a kind of frozen caring, tangled up in guilt. And that fear of reaching out and not being met is so understandable, but I want to gently reflect something back to you: you've already imagined what you'd want him to know, clearly and beautifully, which tells me part of you is ready even if another part is bracing for the worst. What would it mean for you if you took that risk and it didn't go perfectly — would that truly confirm you're not worth reaching toward, or might it just mean the timing or the words weren't quite right?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe that... but honestly, my first instinct is that if I reach out and he doesn't respond the way I'm hoping, it won't just feel like bad timing — it'll feel like proof of something I already suspect about myself. I know that probably sounds irrational, but that fear is so loud that it drowns out the more reasonable part of me you're pointing to. It's like I can articulate the healthier perspective in my head, but I can't actually feel it in my chest where it would matter.
therapist: What you're describing — knowing the healthier thought but not being able to *feel* it — is one of the most honest and important things a person can recognize about themselves, and it's actually at the heart of what we work with in CBT, because insight alone rarely changes the felt sense in your body. That gap between your head and your chest isn't a sign that you're broken or that the work isn't possible — it's a sign that this belief about yourself runs deep and has probably been quietly shaping things for a long time. I'd love to gently explore that a little more — when you say reaching out and not being met would feel like "proof of something you already suspect about yourself," what is that something, in your own words?

client: I think... what I suspect about myself is that I'm just not someone people actually want around. Like, I can be tolerated, maybe even liked in small doses, but if I actually needed something from someone — if I showed up asking to be seen — they'd realize there's not enough there to make it worth their while. And the terrifying part is that I've kind of built my whole life around never testing that theory, so it still feels completely true.
therapist: What you just named takes real courage to say out loud, and I want you to sit with the fact that you said it — because that belief, that you're only tolerable but never truly worth someone's investment, sounds like it's been a quiet but heavy companion for a very long time. There's something important in what you noticed too: that you've protected that belief by never testing it, which means it's never actually been proven true — it's just never been disproven either. I'm curious, where do you think that belief first took root — was there a time or a person that taught you that needing something from others made you too much?

client: I think it probably started with my mom, honestly. She was always so busy, and whenever I needed something emotionally from her, she'd get this look on her face like I was asking for too much, like I was draining her. So I learned pretty early that the safest thing was to just... handle it myself and not burden anyone.
therapist: What you just described — a child learning to shrink their needs because the person who was supposed to welcome them looked burdened instead — is such a formative and painful thing to carry, and it makes complete sense that it became the blueprint for how you've moved through the world ever since. That little version of you made the only safe choice available, but the belief it created — that your needs are too much — was never really the truth about you, it was the truth about what your mom had capacity for in those moments. I'm wondering, when you look at that younger version of yourself who learned to go quiet and handle it alone, what do you feel toward them?

client: I feel... sad for them, honestly. Like, that kid was just trying not to be a burden, trying to make things easier, and somewhere along the way that became the only way I knew how to exist around people. But it's hard to fully separate it out the way you're describing, because part of me still thinks maybe my needs really were too much, and I'm not sure how to just let go of that belief.
therapist: That sadness you feel for that child is actually really significant — because it means part of you can already see them with compassion, even if you can't quite extend that same gentleness to yourself in the present yet. And I want to gently point something out: you're not being asked to just "let go" of that belief all at once, because it was built over years of real experiences and it kept you safe — the goal is more about slowly loosening its grip by gathering new evidence. So I'm curious — in your life now, has there ever been a moment, even a small one, where you showed a need or asked for something and someone met you there rather than pulling away?
